title: Trump tells U.S. army not to detonate unstable, lead-rich explosives without court approval | CBC News

World·Updated

Trump tells U.S. army not to detonate unstable, lead-rich explosives without court approval

Army argues a controlled explosion the best choice for degraded lead azide; environmentalists disagree

U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday he will defer to a federal appeals court on whether the administration moves ahead with plans to detonate several tons of degraded bomb-making material at an Iowa ammunition plant.

The detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide was initially planned for Friday, but the U.S. army has since changed the date three times following an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects. They had planned for a detonation on Wednesday, saying the weather was most favourable that day.

The army had no immediate comment when asked about the president's social media post.

Environmentalists sued last week in an effort to stop the detonation, winning a stay from the appeals court pending a decision on the validity of an emergency permit approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) that cleared the way for the operation.

Trump said he prefers to take care of the volatile material as soon as possible and that a controlled detonation would be much safer. "At the same time, [I] have ordered the military not to do so until such time as the 8th Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Gov.-elect Rob Sand agreeing to the operation," Trump said in a statement.

If Sand and the court don't agree, Trump said the administration will have no choice but to not proceed with the planned detonation, adding that he would hold the incoming governor responsible for "any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and long-term, situation."

Degraded lead found earlier this year

In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.

According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums' contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.

Middletown, Iowa, sits on the edge of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their court filings that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public.

Officials contend that the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. They said there is a risk that the chemicals may explode as temperatures are expected to drop below -1 C in the coming days.

Lead exposure is dangerous, especially for children

Lead exposure can cause serious health problems, particularly in children, including damage to the brain and nervous system.

The Iowa Environmental Council and ⁠the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter filed the lawsuit challenging the detonation, arguing that the detonations would release a toxic plume of lead dust into the air that could travel 160 kilometres north of the site, depending on weather conditions.

Kerri Johannsen, senior director of policy and programs at the Iowa Environmental Council, told Reuters the army should provide more ‌details about the timing of the detonation, where the plume is expected to travel, and what precautions people should take.

"One of the pieces that especially raised our concerns was the lack of prior notice and the fact that many folks, including state officials, did not have any heads up about this.… There was not enough information being shared," Johannsen said.

Jeremy Atwater, a resident of Augusta, Iowa, who plans to leave the area, is shown at the Augusta Community Center on Sunday. (Jim Urquhart/Reuters)

The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship has recommended that cattle farmers near the ​detonation site move their livestock, feed and equipment indoors, or transport them to alternate locations. But farmers have told the environmental council that keeping livestock indoors is not a viable option, Johannsen said.

The army advised people to avoid the affected area during the detonation and urged anyone ⁠who could ⁠not leave beforehand to stay indoors, close windows and doors, ​and shut off heating and cooling systems that bring in outside air. Residents should wet-clean surfaces children may touch to remove any lead dust once the exposure period has ​ended, the army said.

"The early recommendations from the army had a lot of people sort of with their jaws hanging open.… There remain so many questions about mitigation and protection," Johannsen said.

Jeremy Atwater, a resident of Augusta, Iowa, said he planned to head west because he expected the plume would blow south through his town.

"Anything but the bomb," Atwater told Reuters. "It's just going to be a big problem."

With files from Reuters
summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday he will defer to a federal appeals court on whether the administration moves ahead with plans to detonate several tons of degraded bomb-making material at an Iowa ammunition plant.
